title: Avoidable vs. Unavoidable Difficulty
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Using an anecdote about a North Dakota math teacher who explicitly demonstrates calculator use to his high schoolers, Stuart draws a distinction between avoidable difficulties, confusions that can and should be removed from a lesson, and unavoidable difficulties, structural limits of human cognition that no amount of good teaching can eliminate. He names three unavoidable difficulties from learning science: concentration and effort as a finite resource, narrow attention, and working memory that holds only a handful of items at once. His operating principle is that wherever a difficulty can be removed or eased, it should be, both because it saves instructional time and because it signals credibility and belonging to students who might otherwise assume the teacher expects prior knowledge they don't have. At the same time, he's clear that removing avoidable friction doesn't make learning easy; the deeper cognitive difficulties of building and using long-term memory remain, and can only be managed, not eliminated.
points: Core distinction: avoidable difficulties should always be removed because they cost little time and yield large benefits in clarity, credibility, and belonging; unavoidable difficulties are built into human cognition and can only be managed.

The three unavoidable difficulties he names — finite concentration and effort, narrow attention, and limited working memory (roughly four slots) — are the same cognitive bottlenecks that recur across his other writing on learning science.
Demonstrating basic tool use explicitly signals to students that the teacher assumes nothing about their prior knowledge, which Stuart ties directly to both credibility and belonging.

Practical levers for the unavoidable difficulties include building student stamina, overlearning core material, reducing unneeded distractions, and expanding background knowledge — none of which eliminate the difficulty, but all of which make it more manageable.
quotes: Not all students understand how to use a calculator like the teacher understands using a calculator. Showing students how he uses the calculator and explaining why he uses it this way takes little time but has large benefits for students who are unclear.

So, here's a principle: any time we can remove difficulties from the classroom, we should. And this is because learning is already hard enough. The work of getting knowledge into long-term memory and then using that knowledge successfully is hard.

Concentration and effort are limited resources. No human being can concentrate indefinitely. Some of us have developed our powers of concentration further than others — some are like me and some are like Chris Hemsworth — but none of us can do it forever.
Whether you're an Albert Einstein of the world or a person like me, we've got something in common: there are only about four slots in our working memory.

Thankfully, there are things we can do about these difficulties, such as building student stamina, overlearning core material, reducing unneeded distractions, and expanding background knowledge on a topic that we're studying.
Wherever there's a difficulty we can remove or ameliorate, we ought to.
